headline: Michigan elected the first Muslim senator.
summary: Abdul El-Sayed beat Mike Rogers for Michigan's open Senate seat, the AP projects, and will be the first Muslim to sit in the Senate. He is a doctor who ran Detroit's health department. Trump questioned his loyalty to the country in the final stretch; El-Sayed rejected it. Michigan voted for Trump two years ago.

cover_question.q: Why is being Muslim a big deal?

cover_answer: A first. He was attacked over it and won anyway.
table_question: Does it matter that someone is the first, or just that they're good?

5-7.script: A doctor named Abdul El-Sayed won a vote in Michigan, so he gets a seat in the Senate, where the country's rules get made. He is Muslim, and nobody Muslim has ever had one of those seats. Picture a row of chairs older than Grandma, and a new kind of person just sat down in one. Good news, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: A chair in a row is a first they can see. Religion stays a plain fact, like a name. At six they take your tone as the verdict, so sound glad.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole thing, so the script gives them a row of old chairs and a new person in one. Being Muslim is said flat, like a name, because they read your face before your words and a careful voice says something is wrong. Expect "what's a Muslim?" One sentence, then on.

8-12.script: Michigan's Senate seat came open when Gary Peters retired. Abdul El-Sayed beat Mike Rogers for it, so he will be the first Muslim senator. Trump questioned his loyalty; Axios says the claims had nothing behind them. The vote is the referee, and it picked him.
8-12.why: One chain: an open seat, an attack, a result the vote settled. Fair is their subject at nine, and a failed attack is a call they can make.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out rules and whether adults keep them, so the script hands them a chain: an open seat, a race, a late attack with nothing behind it, and the voters' answer. The referee is the vote. Expect "why did Trump say that?" Say Axios calls it unsubstantiated and let them weigh it.

13-17.script: Trump said Abdul El-Sayed might not be loyal to the country; Axios calls the claims unsubstantiated. Michigan elected him anyway. Does winning answer an attack like that, or does it still land? Second: Haley Stevens lost the primary to him, then backed the Republican. Who was she loyal to?
13-17.why: Two loyalty questions, one to a country, one to a party. At thirteen they can hold both, and will want to rank them.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: a man was attacked over his faith, and he won. The script asks whether the second cancels the first, then hands them Stevens, who lost to him and backed Rogers, and asks what she owed. Expect "would you have backed Rogers?" Answer straight; they are watching.

5-7.a: A person whose religion is Islam. Some families pray in a church, some in a mosque.

8-12.q: What does a senator actually do?
8-12.a: Votes on the country's laws in Washington for Michigan.

8-12.q: Why did a Democrat back the Republican?
8-12.a: She lost the primary to him, then backed Rogers. Her staff quit.

13-17.q: Why is being Muslim a big deal?
13-17.a: A first. He was attacked over it and won anyway.

13-17.q: Was Trump right to question his loyalty?
13-17.a: Axios calls the claims unsubstantiated. El-Sayed rejected them.
